reason: The DSHS page lists age 18+, a diploma or GED, a DSHS-approved course, passing the National Registry exam and fingerprints for a Texas/FBI check. 25 TAC 157.33(a)(2)(A), (a)(4) and (d)(1) add the foreign-transcript evaluation, the jurisprudence exam and the two-year deadline. The jurisprudence exam appears only in the rule, not on the DSHS page. Currency caveat: the Cornell copy carries amendments only through 12/5/2019, and its $60 fee differs from the $64 on the DSHS page. DSHS has also posted a DRAFT 2026 rules resource document (proposed changes, not in force), so the rule text may be revised.
found: (4) The candidate has completed a state approved jurisprudence examination ... (d)(1) An initial candidate for certification shall complete all requirements for certification no later than two years after the candidate's course completion date.

reason: The amounts are correct: NREMT $104, DSHS page $64, Cornell rule copy $60. But the National Registry is not a government body, so calling its fee a 'government fee' is wrong. The NREMT fee is charged per exam attempt. And 'the fees are' implies a complete list, yet DSHS says applicants also pay the fingerprinting (IdentoGO) fees.
found: The EMT application fee is $104. The fee is charged for each examination attempt ... | ECA or EMT $64 | Any fees associated with this process will be your responsibility.
suggested_fix: Initial EMT certification fees include the National Registry (a non-government certifying body) application fee of $104 per exam attempt and the DSHS application fee of $64 per the DSHS page ($60 in the 2019 rule text on Cornell LII), plus the applicant-paid fingerprinting fee.

reason: The prescreening before enrolment and the nonrefundable $50 fee are stated in 157.37(c). The case-by-case review under (e)(1)-(3) applies only to offenses other than those in (e)(5). For (e)(5) offenses (murder, aggravated sexual assault, offenses requiring sex-offender registration, etc., on or after 9/1/2009), denial or disqualification is mandatory. So the claim overstates how far case-by-case review reaches. The rule text dates from 2010.
found: (5) A person shall be disqualified from eligibility to acquire an EMS certification, or a person's initial or renewal application ... shall be denied ... if the petitioner ... is convicted of ... on or after September 1, 2009, for: (A) ... murder; capital murder; indecency with a child ...
suggested_fix: DSHS may provide a criminal-history prescreening before someone enrols, for a nonrefundable $50 fee. It weighs most EMS-related offenses case by case, but certain serious offenses (e.g., murder, aggravated sexual assault, offenses requiring sex-offender registration) committed on or after September 1, 2009 require mandatory denial.

reason: The TDLR parts are supported by the TDLR news release (effective January 26, 2026; 8 U.S.C. 1621) and the TDLR FAQ (no SSN means a status form plus lawful-presence proof). The NREMT page says only that the profile 'displays the last 4 digits of the social security number associated with that account'. It does not say every account must be tied to an SSN. A Massachusetts OEMS FAQ found in search refers to an NREMT-assigned pseudo SSN for applicants without one.
found: It also displays the last 4 digits of the social security number associated with that account.
suggested_fix: Since January 26, 2026, TDLR (a different Texas licensing agency, not DSHS) requires certain applicants to show lawful presence, citing 8 U.S.C. 1621, and asks applicants without an SSN for proof of lawful presence; the NREMT profile displays the last 4 digits of the SSN associated with an account, though the cited page does not say an SSN is mandatory.
